title: What is known about 1RB1RC_1LC0RE_1LD0LB_1RA1LC_1RA0RF_---0RC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RC_1LC0RE_1LD0LB_1RA1LC_1RA0RF_---0RC.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and looks out of reach. The machine applies one fixed map, sweep after sweep, to the region behind a block of 1s that grows by two each sweep; the region is a chaotic counter eating a reservoir. Each time the counter reaches the far end (so far after sweeps 5, 9, 29, 137 and 167,887) the block becomes a new reservoir: the last one has 335,504 cells, and at the measured 17 cells per doubling the next contact is about 219,000 sweeps away. The counter has no regular digits, so that contact cannot be predicted; in scaled-down models about one contact in four halts.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 36,772 cells have been visited and 21,796 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 1.1·10<sup>11</sup> steps
claims.text: Direct C simulation, which includes the event after visit 167,887.

claims.title: The sweep map ignores the block; the events
claims.text: At each visit of the left end in state D the tape is D>0 1^n R. The visit-level simulator memosim (8 block cells and R, the rest by formula) agrees with the direct run in block, R and step count at each of 20,000 visits after visit 200. Events after visits 5, 9, 29, 137 and 167,887: at the last one the block is 1335,500, the head leaves the region in state C at step 84,443,579,279, and the new region is 167,752 pairs 01 plus a 305-cell tail (335,809 cells).

claims.title: Next event about 2<sup>19,000</sup> sweeps away
claims.text: The deepest cell reached advances about 17 cells per doubling of the number of sweeps (the depth of a sweep has a smooth geometric distribution), with 335,504 cells of reservoir to go.

claims.title: In short-block models, contacts halt about one time in four
claims.text: The real machine with the block cut back to 4 cells at every visit, from random regions: all of 2,000 runs (8 pairs) halt within 8 events and all of 500 (16 pairs) within 13, always with blank tape right of the head.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: The head sweeps across the whole tape and adds two cells per sweep at the left end, so the tape grows like the square root of the step count.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The counter was not decoded: unlike the sibling ..._1RA1RF_---1RD, whose reservoir is a chain of independent mod-4 counters, no block of this region evolves on its own. Not proved either: that a halt can only happen at the far end.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, and it may stay that way. This machine keeps a block of ones that grows at every sweep and, behind it, a region that changes like a scrambled odometer eating a reservoir. Only when the reservoir is used up can the machine stop, and each time that moment has passed the next one is unimaginably further away. This page runs the real machine in your browser and explains the pieces.

sections.heading: A growing block, a busy counter, and a reservoir
html: Run the simulator for a while and look at the tape each time the head reaches the left end. It always has the same four parts: a long uniform block 1n that grows by a fixed amount every sweep; next to it a short stretch that changes from sweep to sweep and looks random; then a long, regular reservoir; and at the far end an old region that never changes.

<svg viewBox="0 0 580 70" role="img" aria-label="The tape: a growing uniform block, an active counter region, a reservoir it eats, and a frozen old region" style="width:100%;max-width:620px;height:auto"><g font-family="var(--body)" font-size="11" fill="var(--fg2)"><text x="10" y="14">← grows 2 cells a sweep</text><text x="14" y="60">growing block</text><text x="184" y="60">active counter</text><text x="274" y="60">reservoir</text><text x="484" y="60">frozen</text></g><rect x="10" y="20" width="170" height="22" fill="var(--ink)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="180" y="20" width="90" height="22" fill="var(--heur-bg)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="270" y="20" width="210" height="22" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="480" y="20" width="90" height="22" fill="var(--sunk)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/></svg>

The head sweeps across the whole tape every time, which is why the visited part grows like the square root of the step count. Crossing the uniform block does nothing but cost time: the tape the head brings back does not depend on how long the block is. So from sweep to sweep the machine applies one fixed map to the part of the tape after the block, whose length stays exactly the same for long stretches of time.

Here the block is 1n at the left end, the reservoir is a run of pairs 01 and behind it sits a short tail made from the previous region. From sweep 138 to sweep 167,887 the part after the block was exactly 303 cells long; since then it has 335,809. An exact sweep-level simulator that keeps only this part (and counts the block by formula) reproduces the real run, step counts included.

sections.heading: A counter with no digits
html: The busy stretch behaves like an odometer: cells next to the block change at almost every sweep, deeper ones more and more rarely, and the deepest cell ever touched moves into the reservoir by about 17 cells each time the number of sweeps doubles. So eating a reservoir takes a number of sweeps exponential in its length.

For a sister machine the odometer is a real one: its reservoir is a row of independent little counters that each go 0, 1, 2, 3, and its future can be computed far ahead. Here it is not. No group of cells keeps its own count; how deep a sweep goes looks like a run of coin tosses. So the machine can only be followed by running it.

When the counter reaches the far end, the head comes home in a different state and turns the whole block into a fresh reservoir (an event), and a new block starts from two cells. Events so far: after sweeps 5, 9, 29, 137 and 167,887. The last one, at step 84,443,579,279, left a reservoir of 335,504 cells, which will last about 219,000 sweeps.

sections.heading: A coin toss, repeated at ever longer intervals
html: Between two events nothing can go wrong: the machine sweeps, the block grows, the counter eats a little more reservoir. Everything is decided in the few sweeps in which the counter touches the far end of the tape. Each such contact either stops the machine or turns the block into the next reservoir, which is as long as the block had become, so the next contact is exponentially further away than the last one, and the one after that exponentially further again.

<svg viewBox="0 0 580 96" role="img" aria-label="Epochs: each reservoir is as long as the block was at the previous event, so each epoch is exponentially longer than the one before" style="width:100%;max-width:620px;height:auto"><g font-family="var(--body)" font-size="11" fill="var(--fg2)"><text x="10" y="14">epoch k: reservoir of L cells</text><text x="10" y="58">epoch k+1: reservoir of about 2^(L/c) cells</text><text x="300" y="36">eaten in about 2^(L/c) sweeps</text></g><rect x="10" y="20" width="60" height="18" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="70" y="20" width="14" height="18" fill="var(--sunk)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="10" y="64" width="520" height="18" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="530" y="64" width="14" height="18" fill="var(--sunk)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><circle cx="84" cy="29" r="4" fill="var(--head)"/><circle cx="544" cy="73" r="4" fill="var(--head)"/></svg>

Machines like this are called cryptids in the Busy Beaver community: their fate hangs on an unbounded sequence of yes/no questions about a pseudo-random process, and no known method answers all of them at once.

To guess the odds, one can shrink the machine: keep the block at four cells, so that reservoirs stay short and contacts come quickly. From thousands of random starting regions, every such run eventually halts, always at the blank far end of the tape, and about a quarter of the contacts are fatal. If the real contacts are like that, the machine halts with probability 1, after a number of steps that is a tower of exponentials.

sections.heading: What was checked, and how
html:
• The sweep-level simulator reproduces the block, the region and the exact step count of the real machine at each of 20,000 consecutive sweeps, and finds the event after sweep 167,887 at the same step with and without its shortcut table; the direct run confirms it.
  • The speed of the counter was measured from fresh reservoirs of several lengths.
  • Not proved: that the machine cannot halt in the middle of the tape. It has never been seen to, in the real run or in any model run.

family: chaotic counter eating a reservoir (cryptid-like; events at far-end contacts)
summary: A chaotic counter eats a reservoir behind a growing block; far-end contacts (events) after sweeps 5, 9, 29, 137 and 167,887 (step 84,443,579,279) did not halt, the next is about 2^19,000 sweeps away, and in short-block models about a quarter of contacts halt.
